claim: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems are the most closely related to the ancestral system from which all class I systems have evolved.
source: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems are the most closely related to the ancestral system from which all class I systems have evolved and are arguably the most complex (Mohanraju et al., 2016; Koonin and Makarova, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mohanraju et al., 2016 and Koonin and Makarova, 2022.

claim: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems are arguably the most complex.
source: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems are the most closely related to the ancestral system from which all class I systems have evolved and are arguably the most complex (Mohanraju et al., 2016; Koonin and Makarova, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mohanraju et al., 2016 and Koonin and Makarova, 2022.

claim: Type III systems typically utilize multi-subunit effector complexes that recognize foreign RNA and coordinate a sophisticated immune response that results in the destruction of the invading RNA and DNA.
source: Type III systems typically utilize multi-subunit effector complexes that recognize foreign RNA and coordinate a sophisticated immune response that results in the destruction of the invading RNA and DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about type III CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: Of the six subtypes currently identified (A–F), types III-A and III-B are the best characterized.
source: Of the six subtypes currently identified (A–F), types III-A and III-B are the best characterized.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about type III CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: crRNA binding to a complementary transcript triggers target RNA shredding by Cas7/Csm3/Cmr4.
source: In these systems, crRNA binding to a complementary transcript triggers at least three catalytic activities by members of the effector complex: target RNA shredding by Cas7/Csm3/Cmr4 (Hale et al., 2009; Staals et al., 2013; Staals et al., 2014; Samai et al., 2015; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), nonspecific DNA degradation by Cas10 (Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Elmore et al., 2016), and Cas10-catalyzed production of cyclic-oligoadenylates (cOAs), second-messenger molecules that bind and stimulate accessory nucleases outside of the effector complex (Niewoehner et al., 2017; Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018; Nasef et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Hale et al., 2009; Staals et al., 2013; Staals et al., 2014; Samai et al., 2015; Tamulaitis et al., 2014.

claim: crRNA binding to a complementary transcript triggers nonspecific DNA degradation by Cas10.
source: In these systems, crRNA binding to a complementary transcript triggers at least three catalytic activities by members of the effector complex: target RNA shredding by Cas7/Csm3/Cmr4 (Hale et al., 2009; Staals et al., 2013; Staals et al., 2014; Samai et al., 2015; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), nonspecific DNA degradation by Cas10 (Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Elmore et al., 2016), and Cas10-catalyzed production of cyclic-oligoadenylates (cOAs), second-messenger molecules that bind and stimulate accessory nucleases outside of the effector complex (Niewoehner et al., 2017; Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018; Nasef et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Elmore et al., 2016.

claim: crRNA binding to a complementary transcript triggers Cas10-catalyzed production of cyclic-oligoadenylates (cOAs).
source: In these systems, crRNA binding to a complementary transcript triggers at least three catalytic activities by members of the effector complex: target RNA shredding by Cas7/Csm3/Cmr4 (Hale et al., 2009; Staals et al., 2013; Staals et al., 2014; Samai et al., 2015; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), nonspecific DNA degradation by Cas10 (Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Elmore et al., 2016), and Cas10-catalyzed production of cyclic-oligoadenylates (cOAs), second-messenger molecules that bind and stimulate accessory nucleases outside of the effector complex (Niewoehner et al., 2017; Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018; Nasef et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Niewoehner et al., 2017; Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018; Nasef et al., 2019.

claim: Cyclic-oligoadenylates (cOAs) are second-messenger molecules that bind and stimulate accessory nucleases outside of the effector complex.
source: In these systems, crRNA binding to a complementary transcript triggers at least three catalytic activities by members of the effector complex: target RNA shredding by Cas7/Csm3/Cmr4 (Hale et al., 2009; Staals et al., 2013; Staals et al., 2014; Samai et al., 2015; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), nonspecific DNA degradation by Cas10 (Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Elmore et al., 2016), and Cas10-catalyzed production of cyclic-oligoadenylates (cOAs), second-messenger molecules that bind and stimulate accessory nucleases outside of the effector complex (Niewoehner et al., 2017; Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018; Nasef et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Niewoehner et al., 2017; Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018; Nasef et al., 2019.

claim: Accessory nucleases typically possess CRISPR-associated Rossman Fold (CARF) domains to which cOAs bind.
source: Such accessory nucleases typically possess CRISPR-associated Rossman Fold (CARF) domains to which cOAs bind and are encoded within or proximal to the type III CRISPR-Cas locus (Shmakov et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2019; Makarova et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shmakov et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2019; Makarova et al., 2020a.

claim: Accessory nucleases are encoded within or proximal to the type III CRISPR-Cas locus.
source: Such accessory nucleases typically possess CRISPR-associated Rossman Fold (CARF) domains to which cOAs bind and are encoded within or proximal to the type III CRISPR-Cas locus (Shmakov et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2019; Makarova et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shmakov et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2019; Makarova et al., 2020a.

claim: Recent studies have relied upon CARF domains and proximity to the CRISPR-Cas locus to discover new cOA-responsive accessory nucleases.
source: Indeed, recent studies have relied upon these two features to discover new cOA-responsive accessory nucleases and validate their contributions to type III defense (Han et al., 2018; Athukoralage et al., 2019; McMahon et al., 2020; Rostøl et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Han et al., 2018; Athukoralage et al., 2019; McMahon et al., 2020; Rostøl et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021.

claim: The type III-A CRISPR-Cas system in Staphylococcus epidermidis employs the housekeeping nucleases PNPase and RNase J2 during multiple steps in the immunity pathway.
source: Our previous work showed that the type III-A CRISPR-Cas system in Staphylococcus epidermidis (herein referred to as CRISPR-Cas10) employs the 'housekeeping' nucleases PNPase and RNase J2 during multiple steps in the immunity pathway (Walker et al., 2017; Chou-Zheng and Hatoum-Aslan, 2019; Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2017 and Chou-Zheng and Hatoum-Aslan, 2019, and references to Figure 1A-C.

claim: Cas6 cleaves pre-crRNAs within repeats to generate 71 nucleotide (nt) intermediates.
source: During crRNA biogenesis, Cas6 cleaves pre-crRNAs within repeats to generate 71 nucleotide (nt) intermediates (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2014), and these intermediates are processed on their 3′-ends by PNPase and one or more unidentified nuclease(s) to produce mature species of 43, 37, and 31 nt in length (Chou-Zheng and Hatoum-Aslan, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2014.

claim: 71 nt crRNA intermediates are processed on their 3′-ends by PNPase and one or more unidentified nuclease(s) to produce mature species of 43, 37, and 31 nt in length.
source: During crRNA biogenesis, Cas6 cleaves pre-crRNAs within repeats to generate 71 nucleotide (nt) intermediates (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2014), and these intermediates are processed on their 3′-ends by PNPase and one or more unidentified nuclease(s) to produce mature species of 43, 37, and 31 nt in length (Chou-Zheng and Hatoum-Aslan, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chou-Zheng and Hatoum-Aslan, 2019.

claim: PNPase helps prevent phage nucleic acid accumulation during an active infection.
source: We also showed that PNPase helps prevent phage nucleic acid accumulation during an active infection, implying a direct role for PNPase during interference.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: RNase J2 is essential for interference against phage and plasmid invaders.
source: While searching for additional maturation nuclease(s), we fortuitously identified RNase J2 as another player in the pathway; however, while it has little/no effect on crRNA maturation, RNase J2 is essential for interference against phage and plasmid invaders.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: PNPase and RNase J2 are members of the RNA degradosome.
source: Notably, PNPase and RNase J2 are members of the RNA degradosome, a highly conserved complex of ribonucleases, helicases, and metabolic enzymes primarily involved in RNA processing and decay (Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020.

claim: The RNA degradosome is a highly conserved complex of ribonucleases, helicases, and metabolic enzymes primarily involved in RNA processing and decay.
source: Notably, PNPase and RNase J2 are members of the RNA degradosome, a highly conserved complex of ribonucleases, helicases, and metabolic enzymes primarily involved in RNA processing and decay (Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020.

claim: PNPase and RNase J2 co-purify in trace amounts with the Cas10-Csm complex in S. epidermidis.
source: Our original observation that these nucleases co-purify in trace amounts with the Cas10-Csm complex in S. epidermidis (Walker et al., 2017) led to the discovery of their additional contributions to CRISPR-Cas defense.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2017.

claim: RNase R is a third 'housekeeping' nuclease critical for type III CRISPR-Cas immunity.
source: Here, we identify RNase R as a third 'housekeeping' nuclease critical for immunity.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is the main finding of the study.

claim: RNase R works in concert with PNPase to complete crRNA maturation.
source: We show that RNase R works in concert with PNPase to complete crRNA maturation and identify specific interactions with Csm5, a member of the type III effector complex, which facilitate nuclease recruitment/stimulation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: RNase R has specific interactions with Csm5, a member of the type III effector complex, which facilitate nuclease recruitment/stimulation.
source: We show that RNase R works in concert with PNPase to complete crRNA maturation and identify specific interactions with Csm5, a member of the type III effector complex, which facilitate nuclease recruitment/stimulation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: RNase R and PNPase are required to maintain robust anti-plasmid immunity, particularly when targeted transcripts are sparse.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that RNase R and PNPase are required to maintain robust anti-plasmid immunity, particularly when targeted transcripts are sparse.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of RNase R alone causes complete loss of precisely processed mature crRNA species and production of crRNAs with a range of aberrant lengths.
source: This experiment revealed that deletion of RNase R alone causes complete loss of precisely processed mature species and production of crRNAs with a range of aberrant lengths.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Reintroduction of rnr to its native locus restores crRNA maturation to wild-type levels.
source: To confirm that the loss of RNase R is responsible for this phenotype, we returned rnr to its native locus in the genome to generate S. epidermidis LM1680/Δrnr::rnr*—in this strain, silent mutations were introduced into rnr to distinguish the knock-in strain from original WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D). The same assays were then repeated and showed that crRNAs in the complemented strain have sizes similar to those found in WT (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: In the double mutant lacking both RNase R and PNPase, ~95% of crRNAs are trapped in the intermediate state.
source: The results showed a complete loss of mature species in the double mutant, with ~95% of crRNAs trapped in the intermediate state (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: RNase R and PNPase are likely the primary drivers of crRNA maturation in the cell.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that RNase R and PNPase are likely the primary drivers of crRNA maturation in the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that deletion of both nucleases results in ~95% of crRNAs trapped in the intermediate state.

claim: Cbf1 is incapable of cleaving intermediate crRNAs associated with the Cas10-Csm complex.
source: Interestingly, Cbf1 is also incapable of cleaving intermediate crRNAs associated with the complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: RNase R and PNPase each cause partial processing of crRNA intermediates on their 3′-ends.
source: In contrast, RNase R and PNPase each cause partial processing of crRNA intermediates on their 3′-ends, with cleavage patterns similar to those observed when one or the other nuclease is deleted from cells—addition of PNPase produces a pattern of crRNA lengths similar to that seen in LM1680/Δrnr cells, and addition of RNase R into the reaction generates crRNA lengths similar to those extracted from LM1680/Δpnp cells (compare Figures 1E and 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 2D.

claim: When RNase R and PNPase are combined in the reaction, the majority of crRNA intermediates are processed to the appropriate mature lengths (43, 37, and 31 nt).
source: However, when RNase R and PNPase are combined in the reaction, the majority of crRNA intermediates are processed to the appropriate mature lengths (43, 37, and 31 nt) with proportions bearing a striking resemblance to those observed when crRNAs are purified from WT cells (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: RNase R and PNPase are both necessary and sufficient to process intermediate crRNAs associated with the Cas10-Csm complex to achieve their final mature lengths.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that RNase R and PNPase are both necessary and sufficient to process intermediate crRNAs associated with the Cas10-Csm complex to achieve their final mature lengths.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined experimental data from in vivo and in vitro experiments.

claim: Csm5 directly interacts with PNPase in a purified system.
source: Previously, we showed that Csm5 (a member of the complex within the Cas7 group) directly interacts with PNPase in a purified system (Walker et al., 2017), and since deletion of csm5 causes complete loss of crRNA maturation while allowing for the remainder of the complex to form (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013), we reasoned that RNase R recruitment is also likely to be facilitated by Csm5.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2017.

claim: Deletion of csm5 causes complete loss of crRNA maturation while allowing for the remainder of the complex to form.
source: Previously, we showed that Csm5 (a member of the complex within the Cas7 group) directly interacts with PNPase in a purified system (Walker et al., 2017), and since deletion of csm5 causes complete loss of crRNA maturation while allowing for the remainder of the complex to form (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013), we reasoned that RNase R recruitment is also likely to be facilitated by Csm5.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013.

claim: Csm5 interacts with RNase R.
source: Consistent with previous observations, RNase R appears to self-associate in vitro (Cheng and Deutscher, 2002), which accounts for its shallow migration into the gel. Nonetheless, we observed that the addition of increasing amounts of Csm5 to RNase R causes the band to shift upward, indicating that the two proteins interact.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The interaction between Csm5 and RNase R is likely weak/transient.
source: This interaction is likely weak/transient because Csm5 must be added in excess (up to 9:1) to observe a noticeable band shift.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observation that high ratios of Csm5 to RNase R are needed to observe band shifts.

claim: Non-stoichiometric amounts of RNase R co-elute with Csm5 in affinity pulldown assays.
source: Consistent with the weak/transient interaction observed between the two proteins, non-stoichiometric amounts of RNase R were found to co-elute with Csm5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Csm5 is enriched with positively charged amino acids that confer its basic pI.
source: Indeed, Csm5 is enriched with positively charged amino acids that confer its basic pI (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Csm5 has two putative disordered regions spanning residues 109–116 (IDR1) and 310–320 (IDR2).
source: This analysis revealed the presence of two putative disordered regions spanning residues 109–116 and 310–320 (here onward IDR1 and IDR2, respectively), with the latter having the higher probability for being disordered (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B using the PONDR prediction tool.

claim: Deletion of IDR1 in Csm5 prevents complex purification, indicating that the residues comprising IDR1 might be important for Csm5 stability and/or complex assembly.
source: We were unable to purify complexes when the IDR1 region in Csm5 was deleted (not shown), indicating that the residues comprising IDR1 might be important for Csm5 stability and/or complex assembly.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observation that complexes could not be purified when IDR1 was deleted.

claim: Full complexes were recovered in the presence of three deletions spanning 18, 31, or 46 amino acids encompassing IDR2.
source: In contrast, full complexes were recovered in the presence of three deletions spanning 18, 31, or 46 amino acids encompassing IDR2 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: crRNAs bound to Cas10-Csm complexes with IDR2 deletions exhibited a range of aberrant lengths with significant (>50%) accumulation of 71 nt intermediates.
source: Interestingly, crRNAs bound to these complexes exhibited a range of aberrant lengths with significant (>50%) accumulation of 71 nt intermediates (Figure 4C and D), suggesting that IDR2 within Csm5 may facilitate interactions with RNase R and/or PNPase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Csm5Δ46 maintains its interaction with RNase R.
source: The results showed that while Csm5Δ46 maintains its interaction with RNase R (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), the mutant has little/no interaction with PNPase (Figure 5B), indicating that the IDR2 region is essential for PNPase binding in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Csm5Δ46 has little/no interaction with PNPase.
source: The results showed that while Csm5Δ46 maintains its interaction with RNase R (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), the mutant has little/no interaction with PNPase (Figure 5B), indicating that the IDR2 region is essential for PNPase binding in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The IDR2 region is essential for PNPase binding in vitro.
source: The results showed that while Csm5Δ46 maintains its interaction with RNase R (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), the mutant has little/no interaction with PNPase (Figure 5B), indicating that the IDR2 region is essential for PNPase binding in vitro.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that Csm5Δ46 (lacking IDR2) does not interact with PNPase.

claim: Csm5 stimulates PNPase's nucleolytic activity.
source: Previously, we showed that in addition to the physical interaction between Csm5 and PNPase, there is also a functional interaction in which Csm5 stimulates PNPase's nucleolytic activity (Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2017.

claim: Csm5Δ46 fails to stimulate PNPase's nucleolytic activity.
source: Importantly, Csm5Δ46 fails to cause such stimulation, consistent with the loss of physical interaction between Csm5Δ46 and PNPase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The IDR2 region of Csm5 likely plays a role in the recruitment and stimulation of PNPase.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the IDR2 region of Csm5 likely plays a role in the recruitment and stimulation of PNPase, while the binding site for RNase R may reside elsewhere in Csm5.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that Csm5Δ46 (lacking IDR2) does not interact with or stimulate PNPase.

claim: The binding site for RNase R may reside elsewhere in Csm5 (not in IDR2).
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the IDR2 region of Csm5 likely plays a role in the recruitment and stimulation of PNPase, while the binding site for RNase R may reside elsewhere in Csm5.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that Csm5Δ46 (lacking IDR2) still interacts with RNase R.

claim: Deletion of rnr in S. epidermidis RP62a exhibits a moderate attenuation in anti-plasmid immunity.
source: Interestingly, while RP62a/Δpnp performed similarly to the WT strain, RP62a/Δrnr exhibited a moderate attenuation in immunity, as evidenced by a significantly higher conjugation efficiency compared to that of WT (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: The double mutant lacking both RNase R and PNPase (RP62a/ΔrnrΔpnp) showed a near complete loss of anti-plasmid immunity.
source: Strikingly, the double mutant (RP62a/ΔrnrΔpnp) showed a near complete loss of immunity, while the complemented strain RP62a/ΔrnrΔpnp::rnr* performed similarly to WT and RP62a/Δpnp.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RNase R and PNPase work synergistically to promote anti-plasmid immunity.
source: These data demonstrate that RNase R and PNPase work synergistically to promote anti-plasmid immunity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that the double mutant has a much more severe phenotype than either single mutant.

claim: spc1-mediated anti-plasmid immunity relies upon recognition of sparse antisense transcripts presumably originating from a weak promoter downstream of nes.
source: Accordingly, spc1-mediated anti-plasmid immunity was found to rely upon recognition of sparse antisense transcripts presumably originating from a weak promoter downstream of nes (Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019.

claim: spc-sub mediates anti-plasmid immunity in RP62a WT, but fails to do so in RP62a/ΔrnrΔpnp.
source: We found that similarly to spc1, spc-sub mediates anti-plasmid immunity in RP62a WT, but fails to do so in RP62a/ΔrnrΔpnp (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: spc-opt facilitates robust immunity in both WT and the double mutant (RP62a/ΔrnrΔpnp).
source: In contrast, spc-opt facilitates robust immunity in both WT and the double mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The nuclease activities of RNase R and PNPase are essential to maintain robust immunity when targeted transcripts are in low abundance.
source: Altogether, these data support the notion that the nuclease activities of RNase R and PNPase are essential to maintain robust immunity when targeted transcripts are in low abundance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that the double mutant can maintain immunity when targeting abundant transcripts (spc-opt) but not sparse transcripts (spc-sub).

claim: Most functionally characterized type III systems generate mature crRNAs that vary in length on their 3′-ends by 6 nt increments.
source: Most functionally characterized type III systems generate mature crRNAs that vary in length on their 3′-ends by 6 nt increments (Hale et al., 2009; Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2011; Staals et al., 2013; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and, while this periodic cleavage pattern is known to derive from the protection offered by variable copies of Csm3/Cmr4 subunits within effector complexes (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013; You et al., 2019; Osawa et al., 2015; Dorsey et al., 2019), the identity of the nuclease(s) responsible for crRNA 3′-end maturation and the functional significance of this additional processing step have long remained a mystery.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Hale et al., 2009; Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2011; Staals et al., 2013; Tamulaitis et al., 2014.

claim: The periodic cleavage pattern of crRNAs derives from the protection offered by variable copies of Csm3/Cmr4 subunits within effector complexes.
source: Most functionally characterized type III systems generate mature crRNAs that vary in length on their 3′-ends by 6 nt increments (Hale et al., 2009; Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2011; Staals et al., 2013; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and, while this periodic cleavage pattern is known to derive from the protection offered by variable copies of Csm3/Cmr4 subunits within effector complexes (Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013; You et al., 2019; Osawa et al., 2015; Dorsey et al., 2019), the identity of the nuclease(s) responsible for crRNA 3′-end maturation and the functional significance of this additional processing step have long remained a mystery.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Hatoum-Aslan et al., 2013; You et al., 2019; Osawa et al., 2015; Dorsey et al., 2019.

claim: Intermediate crRNAs can mediate a successful immune response under certain conditions, such as when the CRISPR-Cas system is overexpressed or when a highly expressed transcript is targeted.
source: Since intermediate crRNAs can mediate a successful immune response under certain conditions, such as when the CRISPR-Cas system is overexpressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) or when a highly expressed transcript is targeted (Figure 6D and E), the functional value of crRNA maturation is likely nominal and may occur simply as a consequence of the preemptive recruitment of RNase R and PNPase to the effector complex to assist during interference.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6D and E.

claim: The functional value of crRNA maturation is likely nominal and may occur simply as a consequence of the preemptive recruitment of RNase R and PNPase to the effector complex to assist during interference.
source: Since intermediate crRNAs can mediate a successful immune response under certain conditions, such as when the CRISPR-Cas system is overexpressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) or when a highly expressed transcript is targeted (Figure 6D and E), the functional value of crRNA maturation is likely nominal and may occur simply as a consequence of the preemptive recruitment of RNase R and PNPase to the effector complex to assist during interference.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the experimental data.

claim: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems rely upon RNA recognition to eliminate invading DNA.
source: It is now well understood that most, if not all, type III CRISPR-Cas systems rely upon RNA recognition to eliminate invading DNA (Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Elmore et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017), and this feature presents unique challenges owing to the fact that targeted transcripts can have variable levels of expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Elmore et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017.

claim: Highly expressed target RNAs elicit a robust and sustained immune response that results in the swift elimination of nucleic acid invaders.
source: Previous studies have shown that while highly expressed target RNAs elicit a robust and sustained immune response that results in the swift elimination of nucleic acid invaders, low-abundance targets evoke a weak immune response, and corresponding invaders are more difficult to clear (Goldberg et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016; Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Goldberg et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016; Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019.

claim: Low-abundance targets evoke a weak immune response, and corresponding invaders are more difficult to clear.
source: Previous studies have shown that while highly expressed target RNAs elicit a robust and sustained immune response that results in the swift elimination of nucleic acid invaders, low-abundance targets evoke a weak immune response, and corresponding invaders are more difficult to clear (Goldberg et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016; Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Goldberg et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016; Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019.

claim: Csm6 is an accessory nuclease encoded in the CRISPR-Cas locus that is not part of the Cas10-Csm complex.
source: In the latter scenario, the Cas10-Csm complex requires the help of Csm6, an accessory nuclease encoded in the CRISPR-Cas locus that is not part of the complex.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Csm6.

claim: Csm6 has nonspecific endoribonuclease activity that is stimulated when bound to cOAs produced by Cas10.
source: Csm6 has nonspecific endoribonuclease activity that is stimulated when bound to cOAs produced by Cas10 (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017; Nasef et al., 2019), and Csm6-mediated degradation of transcripts derived from both the invader and host causes growth arrest until the foreign nucleic acids are cleared (Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017; Nasef et al., 2019.

claim: Csm6-mediated degradation of transcripts derived from both the invader and host causes growth arrest until the foreign nucleic acids are cleared.
source: Csm6 has nonspecific endoribonuclease activity that is stimulated when bound to cOAs produced by Cas10 (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017; Nasef et al., 2019), and Csm6-mediated degradation of transcripts derived from both the invader and host causes growth arrest until the foreign nucleic acids are cleared (Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019.

claim: Once recruited by the complex, PNPase and RNase R likely degrade nucleic acids in the vicinity nonspecifically, similarly to Csm6.
source: Once recruited by the complex, PNPase and RNase R likely degrade nucleic acids in the vicinity nonspecifically, similarly to Csm6.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and speculation from the known activities of PNPase, RNase R, and Csm6.

claim: Csm6 is dispensable for immunity when targeted transcripts are highly expressed.
source: Interestingly, Csm6 is dispensable for immunity when targeted transcripts are highly expressed (Jiang et al., 2016; Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019), similar to RNase R and PNPase (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2016 and Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019.

claim: PNPase is a member of the RNA degradosome, a multi-enzyme complex that catalyzes RNA processing and degradation.
source: Unlike Csm6, PNPase and RNase R are 3′–5′ exonucleases primarily involved in housekeeping functions—PNPase is a member of the RNA degradosome, a multi-enzyme complex that catalyzes RNA processing and degradation, and RNase R performs similar/overlapping functions, but works independently of the degradosome in most organisms (Bechhofer and Deutscher, 2019; Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bechhofer and Deutscher, 2019 and Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020.

claim: RNase R performs similar/overlapping functions to PNPase, but works independently of the degradosome in most organisms.
source: Unlike Csm6, PNPase and RNase R are 3′–5′ exonucleases primarily involved in housekeeping functions—PNPase is a member of the RNA degradosome, a multi-enzyme complex that catalyzes RNA processing and degradation, and RNase R performs similar/overlapping functions, but works independently of the degradosome in most organisms (Bechhofer and Deutscher, 2019; Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bechhofer and Deutscher, 2019 and Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020.

claim: PNPase has the capacity to degrade single-stranded DNA, presumably to facilitate DNA repair.
source: In addition to its RNase activity, PNPase has the capacity to degrade single-stranded DNA (Walker et al., 2017), presumably to facilitate DNA repair (Cardenas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2017 and Cardenas et al., 2009.

claim: Most type III CRISPR-Cas systems possess Csm5 homologs.
source: Given that most type III CRISPR-Cas systems possess Csm5 homologs (Makarova et al., 2020b), and RNase R and PNPase are evolutionarily conserved in prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Zuo and Deutscher, 2001), their enlistment in type III CRISPR-Cas defense may be a common feature in diverse organisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Makarova et al., 2020b.

claim: RNase R and PNPase are evolutionarily conserved in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: Given that most type III CRISPR-Cas systems possess Csm5 homologs (Makarova et al., 2020b), and RNase R and PNPase are evolutionarily conserved in prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Zuo and Deutscher, 2001), their enlistment in type III CRISPR-Cas defense may be a common feature in diverse organisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zuo and Deutscher, 2001.

claim: Enlistment of RNase R and PNPase in type III CRISPR-Cas defense may be a common feature in diverse organisms.
source: Given that most type III CRISPR-Cas systems possess Csm5 homologs (Makarova et al., 2020b), and RNase R and PNPase are evolutionarily conserved in prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Zuo and Deutscher, 2001), their enlistment in type III CRISPR-Cas defense may be a common feature in diverse organisms.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the conservation of Csm5, RNase R, and PNPase.

claim: Harnessing the activities of housekeeping nucleases may have evolved as a strategy to minimize the genetic footprint of complex immune systems while cutting the energetic costs associated with manufacturing enzymes with redundant functions.
source: Harnessing the activities of housekeeping nucleases and channeling their diverse activities toward defense may have evolved as a strategy to minimize the genetic footprint of complex immune systems while cutting the energetic costs associated with manufacturing enzymes with redundant functions.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the evolutionary advantages of using housekeeping nucleases.

claim: Processing of both crRNAs and tracrRNA in the type II CRISPR-Cas system of Streptococcus pyogenes relies upon RNase III.
source: The earliest example of this phenomenon was discovered over a decade ago in the type II CRISPR-Cas system of Streptococcus pyogenes, in which processing of both crRNAs and the trans-encoded small RNA (tracrRNA) was shown to rely upon RNase III (Deltcheva et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deltcheva et al., 2011.

claim: RNase III-mediated crRNA/tracrRNA processing is a universal feature of type II systems.
source: RNase III-mediated crRNA/tracrRNA processing is now considered a universal feature of type II systems (Makarova et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Makarova et al., 2020b.

claim: New spacer acquisition (adaptation) in type I and II systems relies upon the DNA repair machinery RecBCD and AddAB in Gram-negative and -positive organisms, respectively.
source: In addition, new spacer acquisition (i.e., adaptation) in type I and II systems has been shown to rely upon the DNA repair machinery RecBCD and AddAB in Gram-negative and -positive organisms, respectively (Levy et al., 2015; Modell et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Levy et al., 2015 and Modell et al., 2017.

claim: RNase J2 plays a critical role in interference in the type III-A system of S. epidermidis.
source: Also, we showed that RNase J2 plays a critical role in interference in the type III-A system of S. epidermidis (Chou-Zheng and Hatoum-Aslan, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chou-Zheng and Hatoum-Aslan, 2019.

claim: A type III-B variant in Synechocystis 6803 that lacks a Cas6 homolog relies upon RNase E to catalyze processing of pre-crRNAs.
source: In one such example, a type III-B variant in Synechocystis 6803 that lacks a Cas6 homolog relies upon RNase E to catalyze processing of pre-crRNAs (Behler et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Behler et al., 2018.

claim: A unique CRISPR element in Listeria monocytogenes, which is completely devoid of cas genes, utilizes PNPase for crRNA processing and interference.
source: In another more extreme example, a unique CRISPR element in Listeria monocytogenes, which is completely devoid of cas genes, was shown to utilize PNPase for crRNA processing and interference (Sesto et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sesto et al., 2014.

claim: Housekeeping nucleases are needed on a daily basis and therefore less likely to be lost via natural selection.
source: Since housekeeping nucleases are needed on a daily basis and therefore less likely to be lost via natural selection, it is plausible that their enlistment in nucleic acid defense may be more widespread than currently appreciated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and speculation about the evolutionary stability of housekeeping nucleases.

claim: Enlistment of housekeeping nucleases in nucleic acid defense may be more widespread than currently appreciated.
source: Since housekeeping nucleases are needed on a daily basis and therefore less likely to be lost via natural selection, it is plausible that their enlistment in nucleic acid defense may be more widespread than currently appreciated.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the examples of housekeeping nucleases being used in various CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: The type III-A CRISPR-Cas system in S. epidermidis RP62a encodes three spacers, four repeats, and nine CRISPR-associated (cas and csm) genes.
source: The type III-A CRISPR-Cas system (herein referred to as CRISPR-Cas10) in S. epidermidis RP62a encodes three spacers (colored squares), four repeats (light gray squares), and nine CRISPR-associated (cas and csm) genes (colored pentagons).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and Figure 1A.

claim: Mature crRNAs associate with Cas10, Csm2, Csm3, Csm4, and Csm5 in various stoichiometries to form the Cas10-Csm effector complex.
source: Mature crRNAs associate with Cas10, Csm2, Csm3, Csm4, and Csm5 in various stoichiometries to form the Cas10-Csm effector complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and Figure 1C.

claim: Interference is initiated when the effector complex binds to invading transcripts that bear complementarity to the crRNA.
source: Interference is initiated when the effector complex binds to invading transcripts that bear complementarity to the crRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and Figure 1C.

claim: Cas10-Csm complexes can be purified from S. epidermidis LM1680 strains using Ni2+ affinity chromatography when Csm2 is tagged with a 6-His tag.
source: Cas10-Csm complexes extracted from indicated S. epidermidis LM1680 strains bearing pcrispr-cas/csm2H6N are shown. The plasmid pcrispr-cas contains the entire CRISPR-Cas10 system with a 6-His tag on the N-terminus of Csm2. Whole-cell lysates from indicated strains were subjected to Ni2+ affinity chromatography, and purified complexes were resolved in an SDS-PAGE gel and visualized with Coomassie G-250 staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and Figure 1D.

claim: RNase R alone is unable to process about half of the intermediate crRNAs even when given up to 60 min in the in vitro assay.
source: Even when given up to 60 min in the in vitro assay, RNase R alone is unable to process about half of the intermediate crRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The association of RNase R and PNPase with the Cas10-Csm complex is likely mutually exclusive.
source: Since RNase R and PNPase are each about twice the size of Csm5, their association with the Cas10-Csm complex is likely mutually exclusive, and their docking site(s) may also overlap with other components in the complex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the relative sizes of the proteins.

claim: Cas10-Csm's ability to interface with diverse cellular nucleases bears striking parallels to the assembly of prokaryotic degradosomes and eukaryotic granules.
source: Regardless of the precise molecular requirements for recruitment, Cas10-Csm's ability to interface with diverse cellular nucleases is remarkable and bears striking parallels to the assembly of prokaryotic degradosomes and eukaryotic granules, which rely upon 'hub' proteins to recruit multiple members of enzyme complexes through transient interactions with one or more IDRs (Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and comparison to known biological systems, supported by a citation to Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020.

claim: Prokaryotic degradosomes and eukaryotic granules rely upon 'hub' proteins to recruit multiple members of enzyme complexes through transient interactions with one or more IDRs.
source: Regardless of the precise molecular requirements for recruitment, Cas10-Csm's ability to interface with diverse cellular nucleases is remarkable and bears striking parallels to the assembly of prokaryotic degradosomes and eukaryotic granules, which rely upon 'hub' proteins to recruit multiple members of enzyme complexes through transient interactions with one or more IDRs (Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tejada-Arranz et al., 2020.
